newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Peace generally holds in Central African Republic.
newsitem.headline: Peace generally holds in Central African Republic.

text.p: African peacekeepers said disaffected soldiers were confined to a small part of the Central African Republic capital Bangui on Tuesday after four days of clashes.

Residents said occasional small-arms fire could be heard through the night, and army mutineers said two shells fell on their stronghold of Camp Kassai, destroying buildings. They did not report any deaths.

Troops from former colonial power France patrolled the centre on Monday and joined peacekeepers on a sweep of southern districts loyal to the mutineers who have yet to rejoin their units under a January peace deal.

The commander of the African force, Gabonese General Edouard Nkili, told Radio France International most of the city had been brought under control: "It remains only the base at Kassai and the nearby districts ... they are still held by the mutineers."

Medical workers say the clashes, which have included mortar and artillery salvoes, have killed at least 30 people and wounded at least 70 in the city, struggling to recover from three army mutinies in less than a year.
Red Cross workers said they were setting up a camp for at least 8,000 people who had fled their homes to the outskirts and the surrounding countryside.
"Our operation will continue until the return home of all those who have been displaced," peacekeepers' spokesman Captain Lamine Gueye told Reuters.
The peacekeepers intervened under the January 25 peace deal to end political and ethnic clashes between supporters and opponents of President Ange-Felix Patasse in the army.
"This operation of elimination was prepared long ago by elements of the presidential guard and the MISAB (peacekeeping force)," commented mutineers spokesman Parfait Mbaya, on the latest fighting.

Mali's widely respected former military leader, Amadou Toumani Toure, who brokered the January agreement, said on Monday he was returning to Bangui. He said any solution lay ultimately with Central African Republic citizens themselves.
"My role is to help the two parties, the different parties to agree," he told Radio France International in an interview. "The vital role will always come back to the nationals."

The French embassy was hit again on Monday, after stray mortar shells wounded seven people there, five of them French, on Saturday. No one was hurt in Monday's barrage. French troops are in Bangui under a defence pact.

The Bangui peacekeeping force has been touted as a model for a solution in Brazzaville, capital of the neighbouring Congo Republic where similar political and ethnic clashes killed hundreds of people this month.

Mutinies in April and May 1996 in Bangui began as protests over pay but evolved into a movement to topple Patasse, a civilian from the north of the country elected in 1993. The third mutiny began in November and degenerated into ethnic bloodshed.
Most of the mutineers are members of the Yakoma tribe of former military leader Andre Kolingba.
The 800-strong African force includes soldiers from Burkina Faso, Chad, Gabon, Mali, Senegal and Togo. A Senegalese soldier killed on Friday was among the first casualties of the flare-up.
